newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wireless war looming in overcrowded market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wireless war looming in overcrowded market.

text.p: A price war is looming in the U.S. wireless market, in which few players will make money. Too many companies, and too much money spent on new licenses means surplus network capacity, even allowing for user growth.
"Wireless is going to be a bloodbath eventually," said Bill Bane, a consultant at Mercer Management Consulting.

On the face of it the prospect is rosy. Mobile phone users are set to grow from 39 million this year to 100 million in 2002, the industry says. Price falls are expected, but customers will expand usage, for increased revenue overall.

Nevertheless, even as demand soars, there would be a surplus supply if all networks currently planned were built, according to analysts' market models. "The answer is obviously that they cannot all make it," said David Roddy, chief telecommunications economist at consultants Deloitte & Touche.
Competitors without the safety of a niche will scramble for customers in order to repay the lavish outlay for licenses at federal auctions and multi-billion dollar networks.
The dynamics of the new players mean they must aim for a big market share.
Lowering prices will be an irresistible weapon, but an unstable one. "The first shakeout will unequivocally be in commodity wireless dialtone," Bane said.

These companies are mainly found in Personal Communication Services (PCS), of which there will be two or three new competitors for every metropolitan license area joining two cellular phone companies which already compete.

The battlefields will be major cities and the ammunition will be expensive advertising and promotion programs. If customers are able to switch providers easily, it will be wasted money, merely adding to the financial burden.

Already in Washington D.C., the first PCS entrant in the country, American Personal Communications, has had a dramatic effect on wireless prices, which dropped 30 percent almost overnight when its service began late last year.
By the middle of next year, two PCS entrants will be active across most big cities, and the battle royal will begin.

Companies like AT&T Corp, Sprint Corp and the regional Bell group PrimeCo assume that bundling wireless with other services like local calling and long distance will protect margins by setting them apart, analysts say.
PrimeCo is owned by merger partners Bell Atlantic Corp and NYNEX Corp and by AirTouch Communications Inc and U S West Communications Group.

But MCI Communications Corp, through its 10-year reseller deal with NextWave Telecom Inc last week, has stepped up as an almost-national player capable of bundling services, even though it does not own a single license.
Finding a niche is not as easy as it looks.
"The questions I am being asked by vice presidents are 'How do we set ourselves apart?,'" said Jeffrey Kagan of consultancy Kagan Telecom.
"It is very difficult to rise above the crowd," Kagan said.
Niche providers, such as Nextel Communications Inc or Geotek Communications Inc, which are aiming for the mobile workforce, are better protected.
Many others are hoping to support their networks by carrying data or running Internet and other services.
But in this they would not only compete with each other, but with ordinary telephone networks, satellites, wireless cable, paging networks and cable TV networks too.
In commodity wireless each participant has assumed it can take a significant market share, and many smaller companies have been willing to take on steep debt and equity loads.
Publicly-traded debt in the sector has mushroomed to $18 billion this year, nine times what it was in 1993.
"There may be a problem getting finance to build networks and then there is the problem of market shares," said Roddy.

Prices in some spectrum sales at federal auctions went far too high. Bidders in auctions this spring, cushioned by easy payment terms from the Federal Communications Commission, bid almost $40 per person covered by the license area, three times the amount spent in the March 1995 auctions.
They will soon be joined by winners of auctions currently taking place, for frequencies aimed at wireless data and Internet services.
"I think all hell is going to break loose," said Bane. -- New York Newsroom 212 859 1712
